stories.title: Iran says messages are still being passed to US amid war concerns, and other Mideast news
stories.summary: Jerusalem, Oct 26: As concerns rise about a return to an all-out Iran war ahead of crucial elections in the United States and Israel, Iran said messages are still being passed to the US and Tehran remains open to diplomacy. And US President Donald Trump said there would not be a strike against the Islamic Republic “today.” Meanwhile, the International Committee of the Red Cross has begun receiving lists again of Palestinian detainees from the occupied West Bank and Gaza after the Israeli Supreme Court ordered the government to resume sharing them. Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Sunday. Read our full coverage here. Iran says messages are still passed to the US via intermediaries Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, said Tehran has not closed the window of diplomacy and messages are being passed to the US via intermediaries. Negotiations over the war have appeared to stall for weeks. State media said Baghaei spoke in an interview with a German broadcaster. He said the US appears to persist in unilateral demands and that Trump and US officials repeatedly use the phrase “complete surrender," which Baghaei said no Iranian accepts. Concerns are rising among Iranians about a possible return to all-out war as Israel and the US face elections in the coming days. Trump says no strike against Iran today Asked if he planned to launch an attack on Iran, Trump initially suggested that he would be foolish to telegraph that. But Trump then added: “No. There will not be a strike today.” At the same time, the head of the US Central Command, Adm. Brad Cooper, was flying over the Strait of Hormuz and asserting that over 3,000 commercial vessels have transited the waterway with US military support over the last six months. Meanwhile, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu repeated his warning that Iran or its proxies could attack ahead of Tuesday's close elections to disrupt the vote, citing intelligence. “The (military) is ready both to defend and to strike,” he said in a video statement, adding: “You will suffer disproportionate blows far greater than you can imagine.” Israeli broadcaster reports Netanyahu confrontation over Iran Netanyahu and his military chief of staff have had a confrontation over a political directive related to Iran shortly before Israel's close election, a local broadcaster reported Sunday night. The Channel 12 report caused alarm among some Israelis including Netanyahu's chief rival in Tuesday's election, Gadi Eisenkot, who said on X he backed the chief of staff, Eyal Zamir. The outcry reflected concerns some have raised in Israel that Netanyahu, who could lose power after being the country's longest-serving prime minister, might be eager to attack Iran ahead of the vote in an effort to stay in office. Netanyahu described the Channel 12 report as nonsense during an appearance on another broadcaster, Channel 14. There was no immediate military comment. The Channel 12 report did not say what exactly the Iran-related directive was. In recent days, the prime minister has asserted the need to “topple” Iran's leadership. Red Cross receives list of Palestinians in prison in Israel The International Committee of the Red Cross has begun receiving lists again of Palestinian detainees from the West Bank and Gaza, a spokesperson confirmed. The Israeli Supreme Court earlier this year ordered the government to resume sharing such lists and allowing the ICRC to visit detainees in Israeli prisons to assess their conditions. The government had suspended both practices since the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attacks and the start of the war in Gaza. ICRC spokesperson Gilad Grossman said Israel had not yet allowed prison visits to begin again but “we hope that we will resume in the near future.” Israel rounded up thousands of Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza after the Oct. 7 attacks. Some were released in last year's ceasefire, but around 9,000 are still imprisoned or detained under harsh conditions. Riyadh international airport reopens as Houthi attacks persist King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh said it opened terminals 1 and 2 for domestic and international flights, but Iran-backed Houthis in neighboring Yemen again fired drones and missiles toward the Saudi capital. Saudi military spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki said air defenses intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile and a drone fired toward Riyadh. The Houthis claimed the attack. In early October, Houthi strikes hit an airport complex housing two other terminals, killing 17 people and wounding over 330. 2 wounded by debris from interceptions in Saudi Arabia Saudi authorities said debris from the interception of two ballistic missiles in Khamis Mushait and Ahad Rafida governorates wounded two people, a Saudi citizen and a resident from an unspecified Asian country. The Civil Defense said the missiles were launched by the Houthis in Yemen, and the debris also damaged three buildings and seven vehicles. The Houthi rebels later claimed attacks that included King Khalid air base in Khamis Mushait, calling them a response to “Saudi aggression” against Yemen's rebel-held capital of Sanaa. The AP could not independently verify the claims. Late Sunday, the Saudi-backed Yemeni government accused the Houthis of targeting displacement camps in Ras Imran on the outskirts of Aden with three ballistic missiles, without providing details. There were no reports of casualties. The Houthis did not immediately comment. Palestinian officials say Israeli strikes killed 7 in Gaza Israeli strikes in Gaza killed seven people, according to Palestinian hospital officials. Two strikes in Gaza City killed four people, and two brothers were killed in the southern city of Khan Younis. One person was killed in the central town of Deir al-Balah. The deaths were confirmed by officials from Shifa, Hamad, Nasser and Al-Aqsa hospitals, as well as an American field hospital. The Israeli military did not immediately comment. A year since a ceasefire began, Israel continues to bombard Gaza in what it says are strikes against militant targets. More than 1,500 Palestinians have been killed, according to the territory's Health Ministry, which is part of the Hamas-run government. It does not distinguish between civilians and militants but says women and children make up nearly half of those killed. Pope calls for an end to fighting in Yemen Pope Leo XIV urged an end to the fighting in Yemen and warned of worsening conditions for more than 1 million residents of Taiz besieged by Houthi rebels. “The population is suffering from a lack of food, water and medical care,” the pope wrote on social media. Families have begun rationing water and a shortage of groceries has sent prices soaring in the country's third-largest city.

article_sentences: Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a vocal critic of President Donald Trump, was reelected Sunday in a result that provides relief to critics of widening US influence in Latin America.

With 100 per cent of the vote counted, Brazil's electoral court announced that the soon to be 81-year-old Lula had a lead of nearly 4.4 million votes — 51.8 per cent of the total vote — over opponent Flávio Bolsonaro.
The announcement capped an evening of chaos at polling places across Brazil, following a last-minute decision to extend voting by two hours.

Late Sunday, Bolsonaro refused to concede defeat, calling the move to extend voting hours unprecedented — though both he and Lula made the request — and asked for the election results to be annulled, saying they were impossible to accept.

Lula's victory leaves Mexico and Brazil, Latin America's two most populous nations, with left-of-centre leaders.
It also positions Latin America's largest economy, with a GDP of USD 2.6 trillion per year, to remain independent of the US, despite the pressure of increased tariffs imposed by Trump.

Wearing star-shaped red glasses, he kissed his wife.
Hundreds of his supporters began gathering on São Paulo's main artery to celebrate the victory.
In Rio de Janeiro, cars beeped their horns and a woman dressed in red — the colour of Lula supporters — shouted “You lost!

stories.headline: Tracing 7 decades of J&K Chief Secretaries
stories.title: Tracing 7 decades of J&K Chief Secretaries
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 25: Sajjan Singh Yadav, who is set to become the 34th Chief Secretary of Jammu and Kashmir on November 1, 2026, will inherit a long legacy of Chief Secretaries, both locals and non-locals, with some of them, like Peerzada Ghulam Ahmad, Sheikh Ghulam Rasool, and Ashok Jaitly, having become part of the local folklore. Over the years, J&K’s administrative leadership has evolved despite periods of political instability, central rule, and the region’s transition from a state to a Union Territory in August 2019. The Chief Secretary, the senior-most civil servant in Jammu and Kashmir, is responsible for coordinating the administration, overseeing government departments, and advising the elected government or the administration during periods of central rule. As a result, the Chief Secretary in J&K has always occupied a central position in implementing policy and managing the civil service through these changes. J&K’s longest-serving Chief Secretary, Peerzada Ghulam Ahmad, remained in the hot seat for close to a decade from June 14, 1954, to March 7, 1964, while Ashok Jaitly served as a Chief Secretary from October 9, 1996, to April 30, 2002. Recently, as a Chief Secretary, B V R Subrahmanyam oversaw major transitions, including the reorganisation of Jammu and Kashmir in 2019 and the merger of its former state cadre into the Arunachal Pradesh-Goa-Mizoram and Union Territories (AGMUT) cadre in 2021. The Government of India on Saturday, October 24, appointed the 1995-batch AGMUT-cadre officer Sajjan Singh Yadav to succeed Atal Dulloo as the Chief Secretary of Jammu and Kashmir, with the change scheduled to take effect from November 1, 2026, or the date Yadav assumes charge, whichever is later. Over the years, some of the Chief Secretaries became part of the local folklore. Peerzada Ghulam Ahmad, a local officer, is one among such Chief Secretaries. He served during the government of Bakshi Ghulam Mohammad, and his tenure coincided with a period of institution-building and expansion of the state administration. The tenure of Pushkar Nath Kaul, who served as a Chief Secretary from March 27, 1977, to January 1, 1978, during Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah’s return to power in 1977, fell within a period of political transition and the restoration of an elected government after central intervention in state politics. The tenure of Syed Muzaffar Aga, who served as a Chief Secretary from January 20, 1978, to April 30, 1980, under Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah’s government, formed part of the administration’s efforts to manage the J&K’s departments and development programmes after the political transition of 1977. Mir Nasrullah, another local, who was the Chief Secretary from January 1, 1984, to January 31, 1986, served during Ghulam Mohammad Shah’s government, which came to power in 1984 after the dismissal of Sheikh Abdullah’s government, and his tenure coincided with a significant political change in the state. Sheikh Ghulam Rasool, a local professor-turned-bureaucrat, served as Chief Secretary from September 21, 1992, to April 5, 1994, during a period of President’s rule and severe political instability associated with the militancy in Jammu and Kashmir, with the administration facing challenges involving law and order, the functioning of government offices, public services, and the restoration of administrative capacity. The tenure of Ashok Jaitley, an Indian Administrative Service (IAS) officer of the 1964 batch assigned to the Jammu and Kashmir cadre, who served as a Chief Secretary from October 9, 1996 to April 30, 2002, covered the transition from prolonged central rule to the restoration of an elected government in 1996 when the National Conference (NC) led by Farooq Abdullah returned to office. Jaitley was known for his work in rural development and economic administration. Before his elevation to the top post, he had been associated with reforms in the sericulture sector, including the removal of the state’s monopoly over the marketing of silk. S SBloeria, who hailed from Jammu and served as Chief Secretary from September 30, 2002, to July 31, 2005, succeeded Jaitley and served through the end of Farooq Abdullah’s government and the 2002 Assembly election, which brought a coalition government led by Mufti Mohammad Sayeed to power. Vijay Bakaya, a local Kashmiri Pandit, served as Chief Secretary from August 1, 2005, to May 31, 2006, during Chief Minister Ghulam Nabi Azad’s government. C Phunsog, a Ladakhi officer, served as a Chief Secretary from May 31, 2006, to October 31, 2007, during Azad’s tenure as CM. His appointment placed an officer from Ladakh at the head of the J&K bureaucracy. B R Kundal, who served as a Chief Secretary from November 1, 2007, to June 2, 2008. His appointment came during the final phase of the Congress-led coalition government. Kundal’s tenure was short, and the principal administrative context was continuity in the functioning of government departments ahead of the political upheaval that followed the Amarnath land-transfer controversy in 2008. The tenure of S SKapur, who was Chief Secretary from June 9, 2008, to January 31, 2011, covered the Amarnath land-transfer agitation, the collapse of the Congress-People’s Democratic Party (PDP) coalition in 2008, the Assembly election later that year and the formation of the National Conference-Congress government led by Omar Abdullah in January 2009. Madhav Lal, who was the Chief Secretary from January 31, 2011, to February 18, 2013, served during Omar Abdullah’s government. His period in office followed the 2010 unrest and included efforts by the administration to maintain public services, coordinate development programmes, and respond to the political and security situation. Mohammad Iqbal Khandey, who was the Chief Secretary from February 18, 2013, to August 31, 2015, served during the final years of Omar Abdullah’s first stint as chief minister and the subsequent change of political leadership in 2015. Khandey sought voluntary retirement in 2015 after the National Conference-Congress government completed its term, elections were held in late 2014, and a coalition of the PDP and Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) formed a government under Mufti Mohammad Sayeed in March 2015. According to reports, his departure followed differences with the government over frequent transfers of senior officers, highlighting tensions surrounding the management of the civil service and the political executive’s authority over administrative appointments. Braj Raj Sharma, a 1984-batch IAS officer, was the Chief Secretary from August 31, 2015, to April 28, 2017. His tenure covered the death of Chief Minister Mufti Mohammad Sayeed in January 2016, the subsequent period of Governor’s rule and the formation of a government under Mehbooba Mufti in April 2016. Sharma had previously served as Principal Secretary in the Planning and Development and Home Department and as Chief Electoral Officer during the 2008 Assembly election. During his tenure, the 2016 unrest following the killing of Hizb-ul-Mujahideen commander Burhan Wani presented a major challenge to the civil administration. Bharat Bhushan Vyas, who was Chief Secretary from April 28, 2017, to June 20, 2018, served during the final phase of the PDP-BJP coalition government. The coalition collapsed in June 2018, leading to Governor’s Rule. Vyas’s tenure ended amid another major change in the state’s political administration. His term was also the final period before Jammu and Kashmir’s administration was led by an officer from another state cadre, B V R Subrahmanyam, who served as Chief Secretary from June 20, 2018, to May 30, 2021. Subrahmanyam, a 1987-batch IAS officer of the Chhattisgarh cadre, took charge in June 2018 after serving as Additional Chief Secretary (Home) in Chhattisgarh. His tenure covered one of the most consequential administrative changes in J&K’s modern history. On August 5, 2019, the Government of India announced the scrapping of Article 370 and Article 35-A that stripped J&K of its semi-autonomous character. On October 31, 2019, J&K was downgraded from a state into a Union Territory with a legislature, while Ladakh was downgraded into a separate Union Territory without a legislature. The reorganisation involved the division and allocation of administrative responsibilities, assets, employees, institutions, and government functions between the two Union Territories. Subrahmanyam oversaw the coordination of the Union Territory’s administrative machinery during the transition. His tenure also included the period of restrictions and security measures following the August 2019 changes, as well as the transition towards the new Union Territory framework. Arun Kumar Mehta, a 1988-batch IAS officer of the AGMUT cadre, succeeded Subrahmanyam as Chief Secretary from May 31, 2021, to November 30, 2023, after Subrahmanyam moved to the Union Commerce Ministry. Mehta’s tenure covered the consolidation of J&K’s Union Territory administration, the continued implementation of post-2019 governance arrangements, and the integration of the former J&K cadre into the AGMUT cadre in 2021. Atal Dulloo, a 1989-batch IAS officer of the J&K cadre, took over as Chief Secretary on December 1, 2023, and would continue to be in the post till his superannuation on October 31, 2026. Dulloo had served in several departments of J&K, including finance, health, agriculture, and other administrative assignments, before serving as Secretary in the Union Home Ministry’s Department of Border Management. His appointment had brought an officer with extensive experience in J&K back to the top bureaucratic post after central deputation. His tenure covered the return of an elected government under Omar Abdullah following the 2024 Assembly election, the first Assembly election in the Union Territory since the 2019 reorganisation. The administration during his tenure had to coordinate government departments under the Union Territory’s existing constitutional framework while the elected government pursued the restoration of statehood. In October 2026, Dulloo became involved in a public controversy after opposing the introduction of a resolution in the Assembly seeking restoration of statehood. The episode raised questions about the relationship between the elected government and the senior civil service. Sajjan Singh Yadav, a 1995-batch IAS officer of the AGMUT cadre, has been appointed to take charge as the 34th Chief Secretary of J&K from November 1, 2026, or the date he assumes charge, whichever is later. Yadav has served in the Delhi administration and the Government of India, including assignments involving public finance, expenditure, public health, and nutrition programmes. However, he has not previously served in J&K.

stories.headline: China’s Solar Technology Curbs: A Global Warning That Could Make the Energy Transition More Expensive
stories.title: China’s Solar Technology Curbs: A Global Warning That Could Make the Energy Transition More Expensive
stories.summary: China’s solar industry helped transform renewable energy from an increasingly competitive alternative into one of the cheapest sources of new electricity generation worldwide. But Beijing’s latest proposal to restrict exports of selected solar manufacturing technologies raises a difficult question: does China want the world to go solar—or does it want to retain control over the industry that makes solar possible? On October 16, China proposed adding 12 photovoltaic manufacturing technologies to its export-control framework. The measures include proposed prohibitions on certain technologies used to manufacture advanced perovskite and tandem cells, ultra-thin silicon wafers and particular polysilicon production systems. Other technologies, including selected TOPCon, heterojunction and back-contact cell manufacturing processes, would face restrictions rather than outright prohibitions. The proposal is part of a broader revision covering 40 technologies across sectors including solar energy, artificial intelligence and biomedicine. China has cited national security and the protection of strategic technologies as reasons for the proposed measures. The consultation process runs until November 15, 2026. The distinction matters: the proposal does not amount to a blanket ban on exporting finished solar modules. Its potential significance lies further upstream—in the equipment-related know-how, production processes and technical expertise that countries need to build their own competitive manufacturing capabilities. If implemented, the restrictions could complicate the efforts of countries that are trying to reduce dependence on Chinese manufacturing even as they continue to depend on Chinese technology to establish their own factories. Europe: Strategic independence could come at a premium Europe may be among the most uncomfortable cases. The European Union wants to rebuild its clean-technology manufacturing base, diversify supply chains and reduce strategic dependence on China. Yet its solar industry remains heavily reliant on Chinese products and manufacturing capabilities. The cost of alternatives is already a concern. S&P Global reported in August 2026 that European efforts to diversify solar supply chains faced substantial cost hurdles. One supplier indicated that solar modules sourced from Turkey could cost roughly twice as much as comparable Chinese supply, while European manufacturing continues to struggle with scale and competitiveness. Indian manufacturers offer another possible source of supply, but they are not necessarily a low-cost substitute. S&P Global's reporting found that Indian TOPCon utility-scale module prices had maintained a premium of at least $0.14 per watt over Chinese equivalents on a free-on-board basis during 2026. These figures concern alternative module supply, not the direct cost of replacing restricted manufacturing technologies. Nevertheless, they illustrate the price Europe may pay when it prioritises supply-chain resilience over the cheapest available imports. The proposed Chinese controls could add another complication. If European companies cannot readily obtain selected advanced manufacturing processes or associated equipment technologies from China, developing domestic capacity may become slower and more expensive. Existing European capabilities in research, specialised machinery and engineering could help, but they cannot necessarily replace China's scale overnight. For European policymakers, the response may have to be selective rather than absolute: support strategically important manufacturing stages, secure alternative technology partnerships, encourage long-term purchasing agreements and accept a price premium where the security benefits justify it. Attempting to reproduce the entire Chinese supply chain domestically would be expensive. But continuing to rely almost entirely on a single source would leave Europe exposed to future policy changes. India: An opportunity with an upstream vulnerability India's predicament is different. It has built substantial solar module manufacturing capacity and is expanding cell production, while seeking to deepen its presence in wafers, ingots and polysilicon. The proposed controls could complicate this transition, particularly where new factories depend on Chinese manufacturing equipment, process knowledge or technical assistance. Restrictions affecting advanced cell technologies could also make it harder for Indian companies to move quickly into the next generation of high-efficiency products. There is, however, an opportunity. If technology access becomes less predictable, Indian manufacturers and policymakers have a stronger incentive to invest in domestic research, develop engineering expertise and build alternative partnerships with equipment suppliers and research institutions in Japan, South Korea, Europe and elsewhere. India could also benefit if global manufacturers seek alternative production locations. But that opportunity is not automatic: factories require competitive equipment, skilled personnel, reliable infrastructure, predictable policy and customers willing to pay for products made outside China. New Delhi will need to distinguish between capacity expansion and genuine technological independence. A large module factory that depends on imported cells and externally controlled production know-how offers less strategic autonomy than an integrated supply chain with domestic engineering capabilities. The United States: Industrial policy meets technology access The United States has invested heavily in domestic clean-energy manufacturing and sought to diversify away from Chinese supply chains. The proposed restrictions could complicate selected expansion plans that rely on Chinese technologies, including advanced manufacturing processes. For US companies, alternative equipment suppliers, domestic research and development, licensing arrangements where available, and partnerships with manufacturers in allied economies could offer routes forward. But these alternatives may require more capital, additional time and greater technical effort. The challenge is particularly acute in emerging technologies. A country may be able to establish a conventional solar module factory without possessing the know-how required to manufacture next-generation tandem cells at scale. Restrictions on those processes could widen the gap between countries that control advanced manufacturing technology and those that merely assemble products. At the same time, the US could view the proposal as further justification for investing in domestic capabilities. Whether that investment produces globally competitive manufacturing or simply more expensive capacity will depend on execution and sustained demand. Southeast Asia, the Middle East and Africa: Different levels of exposure The consequences will vary considerably across other markets. Southeast Asia has become an important alternative manufacturing base, with countries such as Vietnam, Malaysia and Thailand hosting substantial solar supply-chain activity. However, many facilities remain connected to Chinese companies, equipment or upstream inputs. The impact will therefore depend on which technologies are controlled, how licences are administered and whether individual projects have access to alternative suppliers. But with ownership driven by Chinese firms, the impact is likely to be limited. The Middle East has ambitions to turn its capital, energy resources and industrial infrastructure into a larger role in clean-technology manufacturing. Saudi Arabia and other regional markets could use the restrictions as an incentive to develop partnerships with non-Chinese technology providers, although multoiple Chinese firms are already committed to make in the region. Africa faces a more fundamental constraint. Many countries are still trying to expand solar deployment while developing local assembly and manufacturing capabilities. If access to advanced manufacturing technology becomes more restricted, moving beyond basic module assembly could become more difficult. Regional cooperation, shared manufacturing facilities and partnerships with multiple technology providers may be more realistic than each country attempting to reproduce the full supply chain independently. For these emerging markets, the risk is not necessarily an immediate rise in the cost of every solar installation. Finished modules remain outside the scope of a blanket ban under the current proposal. The more significant risk is that countries trying to build industrial capacity could find themselves locked out of selected technologies needed to compete in higher-value manufacturing. What can countries do if the restrictions take effect? No single workaround will suit every market, but several approaches could reduce exposure. First, governments and manufacturers should seek clarity on the final rules and licensing procedures before assuming that all Chinese technology transfers will stop. Restricted technologies may still be exportable with authorisation, depending on the final framework and individual approvals. Second, countries should diversify equipment and technology partnerships. Japanese, South Korean, European, Indian and other suppliers may provide alternatives for particular processes, although no single country currently offers a like-for-like substitute across the entire solar manufacturing chain. Third, investment in domestic engineering, research and development must accompany factory construction. Process optimisation, yield improvement and the ability to troubleshoot manufacturing lines are difficult to replace through equipment purchases alone. Fourth, regional cooperation could spread the cost of alternative manufacturing technologies. Shared research facilities, common standards, pooled procurement and cross-border industrial partnerships may be especially valuable for smaller markets. Finally, governments should avoid equating nominal manufacturing capacity with supply-chain security. A factory is only as resilient as its access to equipment, components, technical knowledge and customers. None of these measures offers an instant, low-cost replacement for Chinese manufacturing expertise. Diversification will take time and, in some cases, mean accepting higher costs in the near term. The credibility problem for China The most consequential effect of the proposal may ultimately be political rather than immediate commercial. China has presented itself as a major force in the global clean-energy transition. Its manufacturing scale, investments and low-cost solar products have helped accelerate deployment around the world. That contribution is real, regardless of the strategic or commercial motivations behind it. But restricting the export of selected technologies that enable other countries to manufacture solar products risks undermining that narrative. To critics, it could suggest that Beijing's support for the global transition is conditional: finished products can be sold to the world, but access to the know-how needed to challenge Chinese manufacturing dominance may be more tightly controlled. That is an interpretation of the proposal's strategic consequences, not proof of China's underlying motives. Beijing says the measures are intended to protect national security and strategic technologies. China can also argue that countries everywhere seek to protect valuable intellectual property. The difficulty is that solar manufacturing is not an ordinary technology market. It is central to energy security, industrial development and climate objectives. Measures that limit the diffusion of important manufacturing capabilities may therefore be seen as inconsistent with the spirit of an open, globally accessible energy transition—even when the stated rationale is national security. The credibility cost could extend beyond solar. Governments and investors planning factories with long payback periods will have to consider whether access to Chinese technology, equipment, servicing and expertise could be affected by a future change in policy. Even if licences continue to be granted, the possibility of restrictions can influence investment decisions. For countries seeking to reduce strategic dependence on China, this could strengthen the case for paying more to diversify supply chains. For Chinese companies, meanwhile, uncertainty over future technology exports could complicate overseas partnerships and encourage customers to accelerate efforts to develop alternatives. China may still remain the world's most competitive solar manufacturing centre. But dominance in production does not automatically translate into trust in long-term partnerships. opening: China’s solar industry helped transform renewable energy from an increasingly competitive alternative into one of the cheapest sources of new electricity generation worldwide.

But Beijing’s latest proposal to restrict exports of selected solar manufacturing technologies raises a difficult question: does China want the world to go solar—or does it want to retain control over the industry that makes solar possible?
body: On October 16, China proposed adding 12 photovoltaic manufacturing technologies to its export-control framework.
The measures include proposed prohibitions on certain technologies used to manufacture advanced perovskite and tandem cells, ultra-thin silicon wafers and particular polysilicon production systems.
Other technologies, including selected TOPCon, heterojunction and back-contact cell manufacturing processes, would face restrictions rather than outright prohibitions.
The proposal is part of a broader revision covering 40 technologies across sectors including solar energy, artificial intelligence and biomedicine.
China has cited national security and the protection of strategic technologies as reasons for the proposed measures.
The consultation process runs until November 15, 2026.
The distinction matters: the proposal does not amount to a blanket ban on exporting finished solar modules.

Its potential significance lies further upstream—in the equipment-related know-how, production processes and technical expertise that countries need to build their own competitive manufacturing capabilities.

If implemented, the restrictions could complicate the efforts of countries that are trying to reduce dependence on Chinese manufacturing even as they continue to depend on Chinese technology to establish their own factories.
Europe: Strategic independence could come at a premium Europe may be among the most uncomfortable cases.
The European Union wants to rebuild its clean-technology manufacturing base, diversify supply chains and reduce strategic dependence on China.
Yet its solar industry remains heavily reliant on Chinese products and manufacturing capabilities.
The cost of alternatives is already a concern.
S&P Global reported in August 2026 that European efforts to diversify solar supply chains faced substantial cost hurdles.
Indian manufacturers offer another possible source of supply, but they are not necessarily a low-cost substitute.
S&P Global's reporting found that Indian TOPCon utility-scale module prices had maintained a premium of at least $0.14 per watt over Chinese equivalents on a free-on-board basis during 2026.
These figures concern alternative module supply, not the direct cost of replacing restricted manufacturing technologies.
Nevertheless, they illustrate the price Europe may pay when it prioritises supply-chain resilience over the cheapest available imports.
The proposed Chinese controls could add another complication.

If European companies cannot readily obtain selected advanced manufacturing processes or associated equipment technologies from China, developing domestic capacity may become slower and more expensive.
Existing European capabilities in research, specialised machinery and engineering could help, but they cannot necessarily replace China's scale overnight.

For European policymakers, the response may have to be selective rather than absolute: support strategically important manufacturing stages, secure alternative technology partnerships, encourage long-term purchasing agreements and accept a price premium where the security benefits justify it.
Attempting to reproduce the entire Chinese supply chain domestically would be expensive.
But continuing to rely almost entirely on a single source would leave Europe exposed to future policy changes.
India: An opportunity with an upstream vulnerability India's predicament is different.
It has built substantial solar module manufacturing capacity and is expanding cell production, while seeking to deepen its presence in wafers, ingots and polysilicon.
The proposed controls could complicate this transition, particularly where new factories depend on Chinese manufacturing equipment, process knowledge or technical assistance.
Restrictions affecting advanced cell technologies could also make it harder for Indian companies to move quickly into the next generation of high-efficiency products.
There is, however, an opportunity.

If technology access becomes less predictable, Indian manufacturers and policymakers have a stronger incentive to invest in domestic research, develop engineering expertise and build alternative partnerships with equipment suppliers and research institutions in Japan, South Korea, Europe and elsewhere.
India could also benefit if global manufacturers seek alternative production locations.

But that opportunity is not automatic: factories require competitive equipment, skilled personnel, reliable infrastructure, predictable policy and customers willing to pay for products made outside China.
New Delhi will need to distinguish between capacity expansion and genuine technological independence.

A large module factory that depends on imported cells and externally controlled production know-how offers less strategic autonomy than an integrated supply chain with domestic engineering capabilities.
The United States: Industrial policy meets technology access.
The United States has invested heavily in domestic clean-energy manufacturing and sought to diversify away from Chinese supply chains.
The proposed restrictions could complicate selected expansion plans that rely on Chinese technologies, including advanced manufacturing processes.

For US companies, alternative equipment suppliers, domestic research and development, licensing arrangements where available, and partnerships with manufacturers in allied economies could offer routes forward.
But these alternatives may require more capital, additional time and greater technical effort.
The challenge is particularly acute in emerging technologies.
A country may be able to establish a conventional solar module factory without possessing the know-how required to manufacture next-generation tandem cells at scale.
Restrictions on those processes could widen the gap between countries that control advanced manufacturing technology and those that merely assemble products.
At the same time, the US could view the proposal as further justification for investing in domestic capabilities.
Whether that investment produces globally competitive manufacturing or simply more expensive capacity will depend on execution and sustained demand.
Southeast Asia, the Middle East and Africa: Different levels of exposure.
The consequences will vary considerably across other markets.
Southeast Asia has become an important alternative manufacturing base, with countries such as Vietnam, Malaysia and Thailand hosting substantial solar supply-chain activity.
However, many facilities remain connected to Chinese companies, equipment or upstream inputs.
The impact will therefore depend on which technologies are controlled, how licences are administered and whether individual projects have access to alternative suppliers.
But with ownership driven by Chinese firms, the impact is likely to be limited.
The Middle East has ambitions to turn its capital, energy resources and industrial infrastructure into a larger role in clean-technology manufacturing.

Saudi Arabia and other regional markets could use the restrictions as an incentive to develop partnerships with non-Chinese technology providers, although multoiple Chinese firms are already committed to make in the region.
Africa faces a more fundamental constraint.
Many countries are still trying to expand solar deployment while developing local assembly and manufacturing capabilities.
If access to advanced manufacturing technology becomes more restricted, moving beyond basic module assembly could become more difficult.

Regional cooperation, shared manufacturing facilities and partnerships with multiple technology providers may be more realistic than each country attempting to reproduce the full supply chain independently.
For these emerging markets, the risk is not necessarily an immediate rise in the cost of every solar installation.
Finished modules remain outside the scope of a blanket ban under the current proposal.
The more significant risk is that countries trying to build industrial capacity could find themselves locked out of selected technologies needed to compete in higher-value manufacturing.
What can countries do if the restrictions take effect?
No single workaround will suit every market, but several approaches could reduce exposure.
First, governments and manufacturers should seek clarity on the final rules and licensing procedures before assuming that all Chinese technology transfers will stop.
Restricted technologies may still be exportable with authorisation, depending on the final framework and individual approvals.
Second, countries should diversify equipment and technology partnerships.

Japanese, South Korean, European, Indian and other suppliers may provide alternatives for particular processes, although no single country currently offers a like-for-like substitute across the entire solar manufacturing chain.
Third, investment in domestic engineering, research and development must accompany factory construction.
Process optimisation, yield improvement and the ability to troubleshoot manufacturing lines are difficult to replace through equipment purchases alone.
Fourth, regional cooperation could spread the cost of alternative manufacturing technologies.
Shared research facilities, common standards, pooled procurement and cross-border industrial partnerships may be especially valuable for smaller markets.
Finally, governments should avoid equating nominal manufacturing capacity with supply-chain security.
A factory is only as resilient as its access to equipment, components, technical knowledge and customers.
None of these measures offers an instant, low-cost replacement for Chinese manufacturing expertise.
Diversification will take time and, in some cases, mean accepting higher costs in the near term.

The most consequential effect of the proposal may ultimately be political rather than immediate commercial.
China has presented itself as a major force in the global clean-energy transition.

That contribution is real, regardless of the strategic or commercial motivations behind it.

That is an interpretation of the proposal's strategic consequences, not proof of China's underlying motives.
Beijing says the measures are intended to protect national security and strategic technologies.
China can also argue that countries everywhere seek to protect valuable intellectual property.
The difficulty is that solar manufacturing is not an ordinary technology market.
It is central to energy security, industrial development and climate objectives.

stories.title: Accident cover for regular Govt employees raised to Rs 1 Crore; over 1 lakh daily wagers left out
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 25: The Jammu and Kashmir Government’s decision to enhance personal accident insurance coverage for regular employees from Rs 25 lakh to Rs 1 crore under a fresh agreement with J&K Bank has raised questions over the disparity in financial protection available to permanent employees and the government’s non-regular workforce. President, Jammu Kashmir Daily Wagers Forum, Sajad Parry, said daily wagers had been left out of the enhanced insurance arrangement and that their long-pending demand for regularisation remained unfulfilled despite repeated promises. “The government has not covered daily wagers under the enhanced insurance scheme. Our demand for regularisation has also not been met despite repeated promises. Thousands of workers have been serving government departments for years, yet they continue to remain without job security and adequate social protection,” Parry said. The five-year Memorandum of Understanding (MoU), signed between the Jammu and Kashmir Government and J&K Bank on October 23, raises Group Personal Accident Insurance cover for permanent government employees from Rs 25 lakh to Rs 1 crore. The package also provides additional benefits, including disability coverage and financial assistance for eligible family members, subject to applicable terms and conditions. However, the enhanced arrangement has brought renewed attention to the position of more than one lakh casual, daily-rated and other non-regular workers registered across government departments. The government informed the Legislative Assembly that 1,00,501 such workers were registered across departments. Of these, 38,585 were associated with Public Health Engineering, Irrigation and Flood Control, while another 13,616 worked in the Power Development sector. These departments account for more than 52,000 workers, many of whom perform field duties involving electricity networks, water supply, drainage, irrigation and emergency restoration operations. The disparity has raised concerns over the financial security of workers who often face occupational hazards but lack the range of service-related benefits available to permanent employees. The insurance arrangements for daily wagers have changed over the years. While around 12,000 Power Development Department daily wagers were brought under comparable coverage in May 2020, regular employees and daily wagers received Rs 15 lakh in accident insurance protection under arrangements in June 2022. However, when the cover for regular employees was enhanced to Rs 25 lakh in August 2023, daily wagers were excluded from the enhanced arrangement. In June 2026, J&K Bank introduced a separate scheme offering eligible daily-rated, contractual and casual workers Rs 5 lakh in Group Personal Accident Insurance coverage. The latest agreement has now raised the cover for permanent employees to Rs 1 crore, leaving a substantial difference between the two arrangements. The Rs 5 lakh cover available under the separate scheme amounts to one-twentieth of the enhanced insurance available to permanent employees, subject to the respective policy terms and eligibility conditions. The issue also comes against the backdrop of the prolonged demand for regularisation. Daily wagers and casual workers have repeatedly sought a time-bound resolution, arguing that many have continued working in government departments for years without permanent employment status. While regularisation involves legal, administrative and financial considerations, workers’ representatives maintain that their demand for adequate social security should not remain unresolved in the meantime. Permanent government employees may be entitled to service-related benefits such as gratuity, General Provident Fund accumulations and family pension, wherever applicable, besides consideration for compassionate appointment under the relevant rules. Daily wagers generally do not enjoy an equivalent range of assured benefits, although entitlements may vary depending on the applicable schemes and provisions. The disparity has prompted calls for Chief Minister Omar Abdullah to intervene and review the insurance arrangements for non-regular workers. The government could initiate discussions with J&K Bank to explore extending comparable accident insurance and disability protection to eligible daily wagers, casual labourers and other non-regular employees through a supplementary agreement or a separate comprehensive scheme. For workers who have spent years serving government departments without regularisation, adequate insurance protection could provide an important financial safeguard for their families in the event of accidental death or disability. The central question remains whether workers’ families should face substantially different levels of financial protection because of the employment status of their breadwinners.
